sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Shang and Zhou dynasties, the Bronze Age of China
sources.note: Direct curatorial essay read: piece-mold casting; final historical paragraphs date Shang to approximately 1600 to 1046 BCE and Western Zhou to 1046 to 771 BCE. Dates are conventional, not precise uniformly accepted regnal chronology. Old /toah/hd/shzh/hd_shzh.htm and language variants represent the same essay. Map bounds are independently decoded in identities.json.

sources.title: Li and colleagues: A view from the countryside, radiocarbon chronology for Zaolinhetan
sources.note: Full open primary research article read, online January 2024, DOI 10.1017/RDC.2023.121. Abstract, Materials and Methods, Results and Discussion. 2016 excavation; 101 radiocarbon dates; strong activity 1300 to 1100 BCE and rapid abandonment around 1100, with limited later samples. Plant/animal evidence; ethnicity cannot be securely assigned from a pot shape. Phase dates are approximate.

sources.title: National Museum of China: the Li bronze gui, Chinese catalogue
sources.note: Direct institutional Chinese text read. Four lines and 32 graphs. Explicit modern transcription begins 珷（武）征商. The sample uses 珷征商, with the source explaining 珷 as the specialized graph for King Wu. English translation is our literal rendering. We do not adopt disputed astronomical readings or claim that the inscription alone supplies a modern calendar year.

sources.title: National Museum of China: Li vessel, food and form
sources.note: English museum object text directly read. Gui held grain such as millet and rice and warmed food, used with ding. Consider with Chinese Li catalogue as one object-level source work in work-budget-checks.json. Avoid unsupported universal diet and earliest-ever claim.

sources.title: National Museum of China: Baoji bronzes and their inscriptions
sources.note: Direct institutional exhibition text read. Li gui entry: found 1976 at Xiduan village, Lingkou, Lintong, reward in metal and ancestral dedication. He zun entry: early Western Zhou, found 1963 Jia village, Baoji; King Cheng instruction to young lineage members, thirty strings of cowries and ancestral vessel. Public text avoids asserting the contested Jupiter interpretation.

sources.title: British Museum: Kang Hou gui, registration 1977,0404.1
sources.note: Full original museum catalogue obtained through search index; direct opening failed. Rawson 1987 and 1992 comments distinguish rebellion under King Cheng from the initial conquest, describe political/family memorial function and handles. Findspot Hui Xian is reported, not a secure modern excavation. Early Western Zhou, eleventh century BCE.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: ritual altar table and associated vessels, 24.72.1
sources.note: Direct object record read. Late eleventh-century group; claimed 1901 tomb discovery, differing foundries and inscriptions; possible accumulated family shrine wealth. Corrosion outlines permit partial reconstruction only; remaining arrangement hypothetical.

sources.title: Peking University archaeology: 2024 discoveries at Zhouyuan
sources.note: Direct Chinese excavation-team institutional report read, Zhouyuan subsection. Early Western Zhou palace-wall construction established through superposition over early pits and cutting by early burials. Ditch produced 204 oracle-bone fragments, preliminary count 180 characters. These are early Western Zhou broadly; no claim that every feature predates 1000 BCE.

sources.title: Peking University archaeology: Zhouyuan in a century of major discoveries
sources.note: Direct Chinese institutional synthesis read. Pre-Zhou and Western Zhou contexts; named bone/copper/ceramic workshops, water/drainage system and roads. These broad Western Zhou discoveries are later comparative context, not automatically before 1000 BCE.

sources.title: Li and colleagues: Diet and social differentiation in Western Zhou China, 2026
sources.note: Original publisher abstract and section snippets read through indexed result; direct opening failed. DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2025.105478. 82 human/animal samples from Qijia, Dongjia and Yaojia; 77 produced acceptable collagen. Broader 1046 to 771 BCE study; no projection of all results into the pre-1000 map span, and cultural affiliation is archaeological interpretation rather than a genetic identification.

sources.title: National Museum of Asian Art: making sense of the future, Shang divination
sources.note: Original Smithsonian educational essay read through indexed text; direct current URL returned an internal error. Describes illness questions, preparation of cattle/water-buffalo bones and turtle shells, hot rod and interpreted cracks. Shang comparison, not evidence of effective medical treatment or a universal Zhou custom.

batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Single historical-basemaps world-bc1500 feature with bounds 104.324 to 122.392 E, 27.158 to 40.351 N, effectively identical to the next western-zhou outline. It cannot represent established Zhou royal rule throughout 1500 to 1000 BCE.
batchIdentityNotes.decision: Distinct early card; no aliases. Existing related cards are not independently certified or rewritten by this batch.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Conventional conquest date around 1046 BCE; pre-1046 passages explicitly regional or Shang context. Approximate phase divisions, no exact astronomical conquest day. Early Western Zhou archaeological features are broadly dated; later workshop/drainage/diet comparisons explicitly exceed the card endpoint.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Modern scholarly/institutional transcription 珷征商 of an attested three-graph bronze phrase; special first graph explained by catalogue. No invented facsimile or reconstructed Old Chinese pronunciation.
